opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the biggest shift is that research became much more connected to something real. Before large language models, a lot of machine learning research felt like it lived on small benchmarks. You'd tweak an architecture, get half a point on some dataset, and it was hard to know whether it mattered beyond the paper.

With LLMs, there's a clear, shared target: we have models that actually work and that people use every day, and the open questions are very concrete. How do we make them cheaper to train and run? How do we handle much longer contexts? Why does attention scale quadratically, and do we really need it to? Those questions come straight out of practice, and if you make progress on them, the impact is immediate and measurable.

That's a big part of why I work on efficient architectures, things like linear attention and state space style models. In the LLM era, an idea that improves efficiency isn't just an academic curiosity. It changes what's feasible: how long a context you can process, how fast inference is, how much compute a lab needs. That feedback loop between theory, algorithms, and hardware makes the work feel alive.

There's also something intellectually exciting about it. Scale exposes things you'd never see at small sizes. Some ideas that looked great in small experiments fall apart, and some simple ones turn out to be remarkably robust. So you have to think carefully about what really matters: the inductive biases, the parallelism, how well something maps onto GPUs. It forces you to combine math, systems thinking, and empirical intuition, and I find that combination really fun.

And honestly, the community moves so fast now. Ideas get tested, open-sourced, and built on within weeks. As a researcher that's demanding, but it's also very motivating, because you feel like you're part of figuring out something that's still very much unfinished.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that the problems finally feel real. Before large language models, a lot of research was about getting a slightly better number on a benchmark, and you could never be sure whether an idea actually mattered or whether it only worked at a small scale. Now, when you work on something like a new attention mechanism or a linear RNN, you can see very directly whether it helps a model that people actually use. The gap between a research idea and real impact has become much shorter.

There is also a lot more open space than people assume. Everyone talks about scaling, but the architectures themselves are still quite immature. Transformers have this quadratic cost in sequence length, and the KV cache grows without bound, so long-context inference is expensive. That creates a very concrete question: can we design models that keep the quality of attention but have linear cost and constant memory? That is what drew me to things like linear attention, RetNet-style decay, and later Gated DeltaNet. These are not small tweaks. They touch how a model stores and retrieves information, and you can reason about them mathematically, write efficient kernels for them, and then test them at scale. That combination of theory, systems, and empirical results is what I find very satisfying.

And honestly, the community is more fun now. The pace is fast, people share code and kernels openly, and you can collaborate with others around the world. When I started the flash-linear-attention library, it was partly because I needed fast implementations for my own experiments, but it turned into a place where many researchers compare ideas on equal footing. That kind of shared infrastructure makes research more interesting, because you spend less time on repetitive engineering and more time on the actual questions.

astra-6.text:
For me, the exciting thing is that language models have made the gap between an idea and a working system much smaller. You can ask a question about reasoning, learning, or how a model uses information, and then build an experiment to explore it. Sometimes the model does something surprisingly well; sometimes it fails in a way that reveals how little we understand. Both are interesting research opportunities.

And there’s a really compelling tension: these systems are becoming more useful, but we still don’t have a complete explanation of their capabilities or limitations. So there’s both a practical reason to improve them and a scientific reason to understand them. That combination makes AI research especially exciting to me.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find exciting is that we now have systems whose behavior we don’t fully understand. You can train a model with a relatively simple objective, and it develops capabilities that are difficult to predict. That creates a lot of interesting research questions: What has it actually learned? Why does one approach work better than another? And how can we make those capabilities more reliable?

There’s also a very direct connection between research and applications. An improvement in a model’s ability to reason or follow instructions can change how people use it. So you have this combination of fundamental scientific questions and practical impact. For me, that makes the field especially interesting.
